cl_can_smoked_cancer.q: Does smoking cannabis cause lung cancer?
cl_can_smoked_cancer.short: Nobody knows yet. Six studies put together found no clear link; a Swedish study found about twice the rate in men who'd used cannabis over 50 times.
cl_can_smoked_cancer.but: Of those men, 91 in 100 also smoked tobacco, so the two can't be pulled apart.
how: An expert committee reports that the six studies found no clear link. But a higher risk couldn't be ruled out.
The Swedish study asked young men about cannabis once, at military call-up. Then it followed them for 40 years, until they were about 60.
Men who'd used it over 50 times got lung cancer about twice as often as men who never had, allowing for tobacco smoked then. Less use showed no clear rise.
The Swedish study ended before the age lung cancer is usually found, about 70. The committee notes that cannabis smoke, like tobacco smoke, holds chemicals that cause cancer.
cl_can_smoked_cancer.rate: The pooled studies are known only second-hand. The Swedish study asked about cannabis once, at 18 to 20, and nearly all the men who used it most also smoked tobacco. The two point different ways, and neither can show cause.

cl_can_smoked_vs_vaped.q: Does vaped cannabis feel different from smoked?
cl_can_smoked_vs_vaped.short: It can. In one small lab study, the same cannabis felt stronger vaped than smoked, and raised heart rate more, but only at the lower of two amounts.
cl_can_smoked_vs_vaped.but: It's one study of 17 people who rarely use cannabis. Its authors say earlier studies found the two much alike.
how: Each person smoked the same cannabis in a small pipe and vaped it in a desktop vaporizer. Both ways were tested at two amounts, on different days.
At the lower amount, heart rate rose about twice as much after vaping. On the few attention and speed tests where the two ways differed, scores were worse after vaping.
After the higher amount, people still rated an effect when their blood THC was back to zero.
The study didn't test joints, bongs, handheld vapes, oil carts, concentrates, regular use, or the lungs.
cl_can_smoked_vs_vaped.rate: One small lab study of 17 people who rarely use cannabis, at fixed amounts. People knew which way they were using, and with 32 things measured, a few gaps could show up by chance.

cl_can_vaped_lungs.q: Is vaping cannabis linked to breathing problems?
cl_can_vaped_lungs.short: Yes, in one survey. About 1 in 4 who'd vaped cannabis in the past month reported a lasting cough, phlegm or bronchitis, against 1 in 8 who never had.
cl_can_vaped_lungs.but: It's only what people said, once: nobody tested their lungs. So it can't show cause.
how: About 2,500 young adults in Southern California took part. The link held even after allowing for what else they vaped or smoked: nicotine, cigarettes and cannabis.
Even people who hadn't vaped cannabis in over 6 months reported more symptoms. So something else about them may explain part of the link.
The survey didn't ask what people vaped, and it ran into the 2019 outbreak of vaping lung injury (EVALI). So it can't say if those products played a part.
A 2024 review found no study that followed people who vape cannabis over time. None compared them with people who don't use it.
cl_can_vaped_lungs.rate: One survey that asked once about symptoms people reported, with no lung tests. People who hadn't vaped cannabis for months also reported more symptoms, so other differences may explain part of the link.

cl_can_evali.q: What was EVALI, the 2019 lung injury linked to THC vapes?
cl_can_evali.short: A 2019 US outbreak of serious lung injury in people who vaped; some died. Most said they'd vaped THC. The main suspect is an additive, vitamin E acetate.
cl_can_evali.but: None of these studies tested whether breathing it in causes the injury. And other chemicals aren't ruled out.
how: By January 2020, 2,668 people had been in US hospitals with it.
Of those who said what they'd vaped, 82 in 100 named a THC product and 14 in 100 only nicotine. Nobody checked their devices.
Vitamin E acetate, sold to cut or thicken cannabis oil, was in the lung fluid of 48 of 51 patients. None of 99 healthy people had it, but they didn't vape THC.
It was also in 23 of 36 cannabis cartridge liquids from New York patients. These studies didn't look at cannabis smoked, eaten or vaped as dried flower.
cl_can_evali.rate: Patients' own accounts of what they vaped, and lab tests of their lungs and cartridges. The healthy people compared hadn't vaped THC, and no study tested whether the additive causes the injury.

cl_can_edibles.q: What goes wrong with cannabis edibles, compared with smoking or vaping?
cl_can_edibles.short: Different things. In one US ER, visits after edibles were more often for being too high, or for sudden mental-health or heart symptoms. After smoking or vaping: vomiting.
cl_can_edibles.but: These are shares of hospital visits, not risks: nobody counted how many people used each form.
how: The ER was in Colorado. Being too high came up in 48 in 100 visits after edibles, against 28 in 100 after smoking or vaping.
Edibles were only about 1 in 11 of its cannabis visits. So most visits for each problem still followed smoking or vaping.
A dose was written down in about 1 in 20 visits, and couldn't be checked. The authors say eaten doses may have been bigger.
Papers citing lab work say eating acts later and lasts longer than inhaling. A review says the delay may lead people to take more than they meant.
cl_can_edibles.rate: One hospital's records, with no count of how many people used each form or how much they took, and no allowance for how the groups differed. What's said about the slow start comes from papers citing lab work.

cl_can_edibles_labels.q: Do cannabis edible labels show how much THC is inside?
cl_can_edibles_labels.short: Mostly not, in a 2014 US test. Only 17 in 100 cannabis edibles matched their THC label; 60 in 100 held less and 23 in 100 more.
cl_can_edibles_labels.but: It's one test of 75 edibles, not picked at random, from markets its authors call unregulated. Products and rules may have changed since.
how: They came from medical-cannabis shops in three US cities. A lab measured each package's THC; within a tenth of the label counted as a match.
Those with less THC than labelled held about half the labelled amount on average, and some almost none. Those with more held about 28% more on average.
Each package was mixed before testing, so the test can't say how evenly THC was spread between pieces. No effects on people were measured.
Werc Shop Laboratories, which four of the six authors are linked to, paid for the lab tests.
cl_can_edibles_labels.rate: One lab test of 75 products from three US cities in 2014, not chosen at random. It measured what was inside, not effects on people, and can't speak for other places or later years.
